sentences.text: This part combines ST depression on exercise, sex and chest pain type with a thallium defect score and a flat ST segment gate, not as a simple sum; it acts on 116 of 242 training patients, 79 of whom had heart disease, and raises their predicted risk (for its typical patient from about 92% without it to above 99% with it).

Through it, a reversible defect on the thallium scan raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% to about 88%, and ST depression counts far more with that defect, in an uneven way: from about 36% at 0 mm to about 99% at 2.8 mm with it, against about 59% to about 66% otherwise.

Inside it, a heart-rate reserve lowers the risk for younger patients: through it, age raises the predicted risk steadily up to about 59 years (between 57 and 64 years for different patients), then no further, from about 9% at 42 to about 63% at 66 years for a typical patient.

A higher maximum heart rate lowers the risk through it in an uneven way, mainly once it rises above about 167 beats per minute (between 153 and 170 beats per minute for different patients), from about 59% at 118 to about 32% at 175 beats per minute for a typical patient.

sentences.label: Raising the risk
sentences.text: This part adds up its inputs with fixed weights: through it, each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 59% at 0 to about 95% at 2 vessels for a typical patient, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher, and higher cholesterol (from about 39% at 193 mg/dL to about 81% at 308 mg/dL) and higher resting blood pressure (from about 47% at 110 mm Hg to about 72% at 155 mm Hg) raise it steadily.
A flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 79%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG to about 67%.

sentences.label: Lowering the risk
sentences.text: Being a woman lowers it to about 6%, typical angina or non-anginal chest pain to about 22% and atypical angina to about 28%, and through this part a reversible defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 27%.

sentences.label: Rare results
sentences.text: Two less common results also count (the model has little data on this, n = 15 and 17): a fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 16%, and a downsloping ST segment raises it to about 78%.

This part reads age, cholesterol, chest pain type and the ST segment, and acts on 84 of 242 training patients, 46 of whom had heart disease; for the typical patient it acts on, the predicted risk is about 99% without it and about 98% with it.

Through it, older age lowers the predicted risk: nothing until about 61 years (between 50 and 67 years for different patients), then steadily, for a typical patient from about 59% at 42 to about 48% at 66 years.
Through it, typical angina lowers the risk to about 40% and a downsloping ST segment to about 27% (the model has little data on this, n = 17).

lead.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results) the model predicts a risk of heart disease of about 59%; it combines three parts, not as a simple sum: an ST depression and thallium defect hinge, a weighted sum of most of its inputs, and an age and cholesterol brake.

evidence.text: Through it, each extra vessel takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 59% at 0 to about 95% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher; cholesterol raises it steadily from about 39% at 193 mg/dL to about 81% at 308 mg/dL, and blood pressure from about 47% at 110 mm Hg to about 72% at 155 mm Hg.

A flat ST segment takes it to about 79% and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy to about 67%; being a woman takes it to about 6%, typical angina or non-anginal chest pain to about 22%, atypical angina to about 28% and a reversible thallium defect to about 27%.
A fixed defect on the thallium scan lowers it to about 16% and a downsloping ST segment raises it to about 78% (the model has little data on this, n = 15 and 17).
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 242 training patients.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

values.fbs: fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

For a typical patient, the model gives a clearly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient has typical angina (about 11%) than if the patient has no chest pain symptoms (about 59%).

A higher age raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if chest pain type is something other than typical angina (in a curve that is highest at about 58 years, lower either side for patients with chest pain type other than typical angina): for a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 9% to about 53% if chest pain type is something other than typical angina, and from about 2% to about 4% if the patient has typical angina (on the training data only).
